prompt: Describe the dialectical method Aristotle uses in De Anima, specifically how he engages predecessor views while developing his own account of the soul.

result.content:
## 1. Aristotle, Rhetoric, Πάθη, and State-of-Mind Aristotle's dialectical procedure in *De Anima* cannot be adequately grasped without first appreciating the rhetorical and affective horizon within which he situates the inquiry into ψυχή. The πάθη—those affections of the soul that are, in the celebrated formulation of Book I, "enmattered λόγοι"—are not incidental to the investigation but rather condition the very manner in which one approaches the question of what the soul is. Heidegger's recovery of Aristotle's *Rhetoric* as a fundamental hermeneutic of everyday Dasein illuminates precisely this point: the pathē disclose how human beings find themselves already disposed in a world, such that any theoretical inquiry into the soul presupposes a prior attunement, a Befindlichkeit, that the rhetorical tradition had thematized long before the existential analytic of *Being and Time*. Accordingly, (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in the Aristotelian framework, "Mind is not at all pure," for it "is dependent upon imagination, among other faculties, and imagination is, of course, dependent upon bodily sensation; imagination is the Boden of noein" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 118–119). This impurity of νοῦς—its embeddedness in αἴσθησις and φαντασία—historicizes the Heideggerian category of state-of-mind by revealing its Aristotelian provenance; the affective dispositions that rhetoric catalogues are the very medium through which Dasein encounters beings prior to any disengaged contemplation. Aristotle himself, at the outset of *De Anima*, raises the question of whether one should investigate "the whole soul or its parts," acknowledging the difficulty of determining "whether its various forms are different specifically or generically" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 4). This preliminary aporetic gesture—characteristic of Aristotle's dialectical method—demonstrates that the investigation begins not from abstract axioms but from the endoxa and πάθη that constitute the living context of inquiry. Heidegger further underscores this point by noting that rhetoric was controversially placed at the same level as politics, which Aristotle resisted, for "they do not even know that about which politics is concerned; otherwise, they would not have put rhetoric at the same level as politics or placed it higher than politics" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 107). Thus the dialectical engagement with predecessors is itself a rhetorical act of κρίνειν—of separating and distinguishing genuine from merely apparent claims about the soul's nature. 

## 2. Aristotle, Time-Definition, and Temporality The dialectical architecture of *De Anima* presupposes a temporal structure that Aristotle's account of χρόνος in the *Physics* renders explicit, and which Heidegger's existential analytic subsequently radicalizes. Indeed, Heidegger's contention in *Being and Time* is that the Aristotelian definition of time presupposes the more primordial temporality of Dasein: ecstatic temporality, with its futural, having-been, and presentifying moments, underlies the derivative "now-time" that Aristotle articulates (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, pp. 386–387). The innovations discussed in the rhetorical context of 1924 prepare this very insight, for as the authors of *Heidegger and Rhetoric* observe, "the innovations in theory of time division 1 of *Being and Time* represent the very fundamental commitment in Heidegger's theory to a temporal manifold, rather than to a linear sequence of past, present, and future 'nows'" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 124–125). Aristotle's own dialectical method in *De Anima* confirms this temporal dimension insofar as the doxographical survey of Books I.2–5 constitutes a retrieval of what has-been-said about the soul—a recollective movement through predecessor opinions that is itself temporally structured. White reports that "De Anima I,1 is introductory, and I,2–5 follow Aristotle's standard doxographical method of surveying predecessors' views" (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). The predecessors' accounts are not merely catalogued; they are subjected to dialectical critique that exposes their internal contradictions, as when Aristotle tests the thesis that soul is composed of the elements against the absurdity it engenders—"why does the soul when it resides in air or fire not form an animal, while it does so when it resides in mixtures of the elements" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 16–18). 

## 3. Aristotle, Time-Definition, and Within-Time-Ness Heidegger's concept of Innerzeitigkeit—within-time-ness—designates the derivative mode of temporality in which entities are encountered as being "in" time, dated, and measured by the public clock. This notion serves as a critical interpretive lens for understanding how Aristotle's dialectical engagement with predecessors in *De Anima* operates within, yet points beyond, the ordinary temporal horizon. Heidegger insists that "Being and Time cannot be clarified in terms of the 'now,'" for "the 'now' is a temporal phenomenon which belongs to time as within-time-ness: the 'now' 'in which' something arises, passes away, or is present-at-hand" (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, pp. 386–387). Aristotle's doxographical method in *De Anima* proceeds precisely within this derivative temporal mode: each predecessor's view is taken up as something present-at-hand, examined for its adequacy, and either preserved or discarded. Yet the dialectical movement itself—the way Aristotle moves from Thales through Empedocles and Democritus to his own hylomorphic definition—enacts something more than a mere chronological sequence of opinions. It manifests a teleological structure wherein the ἀρχή of the inquiry, the guiding question of what soul is, governs the temporal unfolding of the argument from the outset. Aristotle's observation that previous investigators "seem to have confined themselves to the human soul" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 4) is not merely a historical footnote; it constitutes a critical diagnosis of the limitations inherent in approaching ψυχή solely within the horizon of within-time-ness, without attending to the broader ontological structures that the soul, as ἐντελέχεια, reveals. 143–144); accordingly, the Aristotelian dialectical method stands as both the enabling condition and the object of this transformation. ## 4. Εἶδος in Aristotle and the Contrast with Platonic Forms The concept of εἶδος occupies a pivotal position in Aristotle's dialectical method in *De Anima*, for it is through the transformation of the Platonic understanding of form that Aristotle's own hylomorphic account of the soul takes shape. Whereas Plato treats εἶδος as a separately subsisting, intelligible paradigm in which sensible particulars participate, Aristotle insists that form is inseparable from the composite of matter and form—ψυχή is not a form hovering above or apart from the body but is rather "the first actuality of a natural organic body," as Papachristou reports Aristotle defining it in *De Anima* II.1 (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 1–3). This contrast with Platonic forms is not merely a doctrinal disagreement but a methodological consequence of Aristotle's dialectical procedure: by surveying and refuting views that treat soul as a self-subsisting substance or as identical with the elements, Aristotle progressively clears the ground for an account in which εἶδος functions as the organizational principle of the living body. Heidegger captures this transformation when οὐσία, the being of the soul, designates not a Platonic substance but rather "a being in the how of its being"—a formulation that resists the substantialization of soul and redirects inquiry toward the mode of being that ψυχή exemplifies (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 32–34). Similarly, (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) the two aspects of this οὐσία are "κρίνειν, 'separating' from something other, orienting itself in a world; and κινεῖν, 'moving itself therein,' being-involved-therein" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 37). The tension between εἶδος as universal form and εἶδος as individual actuality—whether man generates man through a shared species-form or whether each form is irreducibly particular—remains productively unresolved in Aristotle's corpus. Accordingly, the dialectical method of *De Anima* does not eliminate this tension but rather exploits it, allowing Aristotle to hold together the universality required for scientific definition with the individuality demanded by the concrete living being whose soul is under investigation.
